utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday the Chamber made an order that the two doctors who are alleged to be treating the Accused be present in court today and the Accused was excused from attending. I see he's not in court today. I'm not quite sure, anybody from Registry, if you are able to tell us whether any of the doctors or both of them are here outside.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, both of them are awaiting outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Besides the fact the doctors are here, there is a document. I don't know whether the parties have received a copy of it from Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour I'm not aware of receiving any document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We adjourned yesterday while we were in private session. I assume we still are. We never went out of private session yesterday, did we?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: We are currently in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are currently in open session. We should be in private session. May we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe the -- I don't know whether this document is already with Registry. If it is not we can put it on the ELMO for everybody to see. It is in English, Mr. Milovancevic. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, can we have a moment to study the document that we haven't seen so far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You're reading the document, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's on my screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have we finished reading the document? Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have studied the document and thank you for this short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any submissions to make on that document, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as this document is concerned, it was addressed to the Trial Chamber, and we leave this matter with the Chamber and we don't have any further submissions to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have some brief submissions. As I understand this letter, the difficulty in bringing Drs. Petrovic and Falke is that there is a perceived danger to the doctor-patient relationship. I would point out that these documents are not being called as Prosecution witnesses. There is no suggestion that they are testifying against the Accused. In that sense I think the Trial Chamber should give some scrutiny to whether or not there really is a realistic possibility of damaging that relationship. The second point is, what is being sought in this case is a delay in trial. The interests of justice are at stake here. As I mentioned earlier there is an impact on the victim community, on witnesses, and on the general process of justice at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black I don't want to curtail your argument. You have made that point yesterday. If you could try to limit yourself to this document, I would appreciate it very much. The Chamber is mindful of what you say, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The point I was not making quickly enough is we think those interests of justice outweigh this speculative risk of damaging the doctor-patient relationship and we think we should proceed. More fundamentally, the jurisprudence makes clear that if the Defence seeks a delay in proceedings, they bear the burden of establishing temporary unfitness in order to justify such a delay. If these doctors cannot come testify, there is no evidence before Your Honour. Certainly the letters that we received do not address the issues of temporary unfitness for trial. Those capacities set forth in the Strugar decision are simply not addressed, and consequently we say there is no basis before the Trial Chamber right now for a delay in the proceedings. Nevertheless, we understand the practicalities of the situation. There is a suggestion here that an independent expert be appointed. We have no objection to that, but we say the trial should not stop in the meantime. There is no reason why this trial needs to stop while witnesses are waiting here, while we have a videolink scheduled for next week, why everything has to stop while an independent expert is appointed, comes here, and examines the Accused. We see no basis for that, Your Honour. I don't know how this has been addressed in other cases but it seems to me that until they can come forth with evidence demonstrating on a balance of probabilities, his unfitness to continue, we should continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. In so far as this document is concerned, I think we've made one point and I would like to answer you on that point. That point is that -- is the perception that they're testifying against the witness, the Accused, rather. That is not what they say, if you look at the document. They say that testifying in proceedings against the Accused. They could be testifying on any side, they could be court witnesses which, in fact, if they did testify they would be. They could be Prosecution witnesses, they could be Defence witnesses but whatever capacity they come in they are testifying in proceedings against the Accused. So I think you sort of misinterpreted their letter there on that point. That is the point that I found relevant to this letter that you made. It now behooves the Chamber to make a ruling. I thought you said you had -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for maybe having interrupted you. I just have a proposal, having heard the Prosecutor's submission. Maybe it would be the most efficient to hear what the doctors have to say but, for the reasons mentioned by the management of the detention unit, I believe that this should be done in private session in order to avoid a possible influence or suspicion that their testimony here will cause a conflict of interests. The Defence believes that this would be the most efficient way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say, Mr. Milovancevic. The Bench, based on the letter that is on the ELMO now, is satisfied that the doctors say their coming here creates an impression that they are testifying in proceedings against the Accused and that that damages the doctor-patient relationship. It is not the intention of the Bench to damage those relationships or to be seen to be trying to damage those relationships. And for that reason, the Chamber is reluctant to call them in. That is why I wanted -- the Chamber wanted the parties to discuss this document so that a decision can be made on whether or not to call them in. Now, if they are going to be called just to come and explain what is explained already in the letter, it seems to me as if the purpose for coming is outweighed by their fear of damaging doctor-patient relationships, if they came for that purpose only. It will be something different if they were coming to testify on the medical condition of the witness. The weighing would have to be re-looked at afresh. For that reason, I don't think Mr. Milovancevic, the Chamber should call the doctors in to testify. I think the Chamber must decide on the further proceedings of this trial based on the document that is before us and the information that we have before us on the condition of the Accused. Now, the report that we -- that the Chamber received from the doctors on the condition of the Accused is very sketchy. It just does not give any good grounds for a conclusion that the Accused is not in a position to understand the proceedings and might not be so for a period of two weeks. That is why questions were put to the doctors. The questions were still not satisfactory -- the answers were still not satisfactory. It was requested that the doctors come here to come and testify and they put -- the hurdle that they put before the Chamber that -- why they cannot testify, the Chamber must now decide the matter on that sketchy report that they gave. The probative value, if any, to be placed on that report is very low, particularly when it is borne in mind how unclear the report is. The report talks of due to the emotional situations in the past few weeks. Now, in the past few weeks, the Accused has been in court here and has displayed absolutely no emotional situation. But then that is not all. The report goes on to say, especially the death of Mr. Babic. Now, Mr. Babic hasn't died in the last few weeks. He has died in the last week. But that's not all. Even after his death, Mr. Martic has participated in the proceedings in court here, and has shown no emotional disturbance. I'm not suggesting that Mr. Martic was not affected by the death of Mr. Babic, but I'm saying he was able to attend his trial for a whole week since Mr. Babic died. The Court can therefore not accept that Mr. Babic's death was the precipitating factor for this temporary psychological crisis that Mr. Martic is alleged to have landed in. If there may have been a factor at all, looking at the time when Mr. Martic displayed this emotional disturbance, that factor might be the death of Mr. Milosevic but Mr. Milosevic's death is not referred to in this report. Not at all. So, it is unclear what is it that precipitated Mr. Martic's psychological problems. The evidence of the doctors, by way of a report, as has already been indicated, has very little, if any, probative value. The Chamber does not know on what treatment in the past few weeks that is being referred to in this report Mr. Martic was on, and what the observations of the doctors were in those past few weeks, and all of these are issues that go to the credibility of this report. The finding of the Chamber, therefore, is that the report of the two doctors is not worth the paper it's written on, and the Chamber has now to decide on how long, if at all, Mr. Martic may be given time to recuperate from his psychological problems before the trial can resume. Mr. Martic is represented by counsel in this matter. The Chamber recognises that Mr. Martic has the right to attend his trial but he also has the privilege to excuse himself if he so wishes, particularly when he is represented by counsel. If he chooses not to attend court because he is unwell, it's -- it is his choice, it is not imposed on him by the Chamber. It will be his choice but he will be represented by counsel in court because he is quite entitled to run his trial either in person or through counsel. The Trial Chamber is not suggesting that he should stay at home, but the Trial Chamber says that is always a choice he can exercise if he so wishes. Out of empathy and sympathy with Mr. Martic, the Trial Chamber will adjourn for the remainder of this week, until Friday, and resume with the trial on Monday as scheduled. Sorry, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think I had finished that point. The matter will resume on Monday, as scheduled. Before we adjourn, one or two things to deal with. Can we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of March, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 9.41 a.m.,
